vignette:
Minh presents as a man holding himself together with immense, invisible effort. At 46, he has the outward markers of a life well-lived: a successful career as a senior software engineer, a comfortable home in the suburbs, and a wife, Lien, with whom he has raised two teenage children. Yet, he speaks of his life as if he is watching it from a great distance, a spectator to a story that no longer feels like his own.

The narrative he shares begins not in the quiet, ordered world of code he now inhabits, but in the dust and heat of Fallujah. He was 23 years old, a Marine corporal, an immigrant who had felt a profound duty to serve the country that had taken his family in. He describes his unit with a warmth that is otherwise absent from his affect. They were his brothers. The event itself arrives in his story not as a linear account, but in sensory fragments that breach his composure. The oppressive afternoon heat. The taste of dust and metal in his mouth. The specific way Corporal Evans was laughing at a joke just seconds before the world turned into a white flash and a deafening roar.

Minh was thrown from the Humvee. He remembers the ringing silence that followed the explosion, a silence more terrifying than the blast itself. He remembers opening his eyes to a sky filled with smoke and seeing Evans’s boot lying impossibly far away. That image is the anchor point to which his mind is tethered. He sustained a concussion and shrapnel wounds to his leg, but he insists the real injuries were the ones no one could see.

After his medical discharge, he threw himself into building a new life with the same discipline he’d learned in the Corps. He used the GI Bill to get a degree in computer science, met Lien, and got married. He found solace in the logic and order of programming. In code, there were rules. Problems had solutions. If you wrote a clean, elegant structure, it would function as intended. He built his life like that, compartmentalizing the chaos of Iraq into a locked, sealed-off part of his mind. For nearly two decades, the structure held.

But in recent years, the walls of that compartment have begun to crack. It started with sleep, or the lack of it. He’d jolt awake, his heart hammering against his ribs, the smell of burnt diesel fuel thick in his nostrils. He began having trouble concentrating at work. A complex algorithm he could have once solved in an afternoon would now seem like an indecipherable language. He’d stare at the screen for hours, the lines of code blurring together, his mind replaying the sight of that single boot in the dust.

His family bears the brunt of his hypervigilance. He insists on sitting with his back to the wall in restaurants, his eyes constantly scanning the room. A car backfiring down the street sends a jolt of adrenaline through him that leaves him irritable and short-tempered for hours. Last month, his son dropped a glass of milk, and the sharp sound of it shattering on the tile floor made Minh flinch so violently he knocked over his chair. The fear in his children’s eyes that day was, he says, worse than the memory itself.

He has become a ghost in his own home. He avoids family gatherings, finding the noise and unpredictability overwhelming. He no longer has any interest in the fishing trips he once loved. He tells Lien he has to work late, but he often just sits in his silent office, the clean glow of the monitor a small, controllable world. He feels profoundly disconnected from his wife and children, loving them dearly but unable to bridge the emotional chasm that has opened between them. He feels an immense, crushing guilt—not just for surviving when Evans didn't, but for failing the family he has now. He is present, but he is not there.
